title: The Sponsor
tagline: Advocacy: mentors give you advice, sponsors spend their credibility on you.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for all Vanderbilt staff: learn the difference between mentoring and sponsorship, how to earn and ask for real advocacy, and how to give it by naming who you speak up for.
heroLead: Advice is easy to find; backing is rarer, someone saying your name with evidence in a room you are not in. Today you learn to earn that and to give it.
objectives: Tell mentoring (advice given to you) apart from sponsorship (credibility spent on you)
Earn and ask for advocacy with work a sponsor can safely stake their name on
Name one person whose work you will speak up for in rooms they are not in
missionTie: Great universities run on trust that travels, and people vouching for people across schools and units is Exceptional Core Operations at the human scale.

agenda.d: The line between a mentor who guides you and a sponsor who backs you.
The work that makes you sponsorable, and the ask that gets it said out loud.
Advocacy is a skill you give: whose name do you say when they are not in the room?

manifesto: A mentor talks with you. A sponsor talks about you, where it counts.

sections.headline: Mentors advise. Sponsors spend.
sections.lead: Sylvia Ann Hewlett has spent years studying why some careers move and others stall. Her line is simple: mentors advise you, sponsors spend their credibility on you, naming you for real work in rooms you never see. Careers stall on the first alone.

source.label: Sponsorship vs. mentorship, Sylvia Ann Hewlett, The Sponsor Effect (Harvard Business Review Press)

sections.group: In pairs: think of the last real help your career got. Was it advice or advocacy? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Think of the last real help your career got. Write down whether it was advice or advocacy.

interaction.intro: The two get called mentoring interchangeably, and they are wildly different currencies. Call each one.
interaction.passMsg: You can tell the currencies apart. Advice is words to you; advocacy is risk taken for you.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: mentoring happens in conversations with you. Sponsorship happens in rooms without you, and it costs the sponsor something.

items.q: A senior analyst spends an hour helping a coordinator sharpen their presentation before a big meeting.
items.why: Generous and valuable, and it is advice: given to the person, costing the giver only time. Nothing was staked in front of anyone else.

items.q: In a staffing meeting, a director says: 'Give the data project to the coordinator in my unit. I will vouch for their work.'
items.why: Credibility on the table, in a room the coordinator will never see. If the project goes badly, the director pays too. That is sponsorship.

items.q: A colleague tells an advisor: 'You would be amazing in a leadership role someday.'
items.why: Warm and costless. No advice to act on, no name said where it counts. Kind words become advocacy when they get repeated to someone with a decision to make.

deeper.title: Why sponsorship stays invisible
deeper.body: Sponsorship is hard to learn by watching because it happens where you are absent, so most people conclude it barely exists and over-invest in collecting advice. There is a second confusion: one person can be both. The director who coaches your slides on Tuesday might stake their name on you in Thursday's staffing meeting. The currency lives in the act, whoever performs it. Track acts and you see who actually spends for whom.
steps: List the three people who have most helped your career, then mark each act of help A for advice or S for sponsorship. Notice the ratio.
Write down one decision that went your way where you never learned who spoke for you. Someone probably did.

sections.headline: Sponsorship is earned, then asked for.
sections.lead: Sponsors back work they have seen; their reputation rides on it. In the research behind HBR's The Real Benefit of Finding a Sponsor, people with sponsors were far likelier to ask for stretch work and raises, and to get them. Your levers: be seen, then ask.

source.label: The Real Benefit of Finding a Sponsor, Sylvia Ann Hewlett (Harvard Business Review)

interaction.intro: Advocacy rarely arrives unrequested. Choose how you make your work sponsorable and how you ask.

opts.t: Work hard and trust that good work speaks for itself.
opts.coach: Good work is silent. A sponsor can only stake their name on work they have actually seen, and seen is something you have to arrange.

opts.t: Send your accomplishments upward in a monthly summary email.
opts.coach: Visible, at least. A list of wins reads as self-promotion; a sponsor needs to see the work itself and what it took.

opts.t: Show one finished piece of work to someone senior and walk them through how you did it.
opts.coach: Evidence beats claims. Now there is something specific a sponsor can repeat in a room: I have seen this person's work, and it was good.

opts.t: Never ask; if they wanted to advocate for you, they would.
opts.coach: Sponsors are busy, and unspoken hopes are invisible. The people who get sponsored are overwhelmingly the people who asked.

opts.t: Ask them to be your mentor and hope it grows into more.
opts.coach: Mentoring is a fine door, and it can stay advice forever. If what you want is backing, the ask has to name backing.

opts.t: Name the room: 'When the project team forms, would you put my name forward?'
opts.coach: Specific, bounded, and easy to say yes to. You have told them exactly where their credibility would go and what for.

heads.strong: An ask a sponsor can act on. They have seen the work, they know the room, and saying your name got easy.
heads.mid: Halfway to backed. Something was visible or something was asked, and the two never quite connected.
heads.weak: Silence, politely. Nobody saw the work, nobody heard an ask, and the backing went to someone who did both.

reactions.strong: Two weeks later a project team forms and your name is on it. You find out afterward who said it, and in which meeting. That is what being sponsored feels like: news.
reactions.mid: Your would-be sponsor thinks well of you in a general way. When the room asked for names, general goodwill produced a pause, and the pause produced someone else's name.
reactions.weak: Months pass. The work stayed good and stayed invisible. The colleague who walked a director through one finished project is now leading the thing you wanted.

deeper.title: Choosing the right sponsor
deeper.body: Not every senior person can sponsor you; the credibility has to be spendable in the rooms you need. Look for someone who has actually seen your finished work, sits in or near the rooms where your kind of chance gets decided, and has a record of saying names other than their own favorites. One well-placed sponsor beats three prestigious ones. And keep the ask bounded to one room and one chance, so their yes is cheap to give.
steps: Name the room where your next chance gets decided, then list who is actually in it. Your sponsor search starts on that list.
Pick the one person on that list who has seen your finished work. If nobody has, your first move is the showing, not the ask.

sections.headline: Advocacy is also a skill you give.
sections.lead: You do not need a title to sponsor someone. Everyone sits in rooms a colleague is absent from: meetings, chats, hallway asks for a name. Speaking up there, with evidence, is sponsorship at any level. The test is whether you can name who you do it for.
sections.group: In pairs: whose work have you actually spoken up for lately, role only? If nobody comes to mind, say that. 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Write the role of one person whose work you have spoken up for lately. If nobody comes to mind, write that down too.

card.text: Whose name do you say in rooms they are not in? If the answer is nobody, you are holding credibility and spending none of it. Pick one colleague whose work you have seen, and say their name the next time the room asks who could do this.

interaction.context: Right now, somewhere at Vanderbilt, a staffing conversation is asking who could take this on. The names that get said belong to people whose work someone in the room has seen. Every person on this call is the potential sayer of a name this week, whatever their title.
interaction.discuss: Whose name do you actually say in rooms they are not in, roles only? If the honest answer is nobody, what would it take to change that this week?
interaction.q: Quick check: what turns a compliment into an act of sponsorship?

opts.t: Saying it directly to the person, warmly
opts.why: That is encouragement, and it is kind. Sponsorship starts when the same words travel to someone who makes decisions.

opts.t: Repeating it, with evidence, to someone who decides
opts.why: Exactly. The name, the work you have seen, and a decision-maker hearing it. That costs you a little credibility, which is what makes it real.

opts.t: Posting public praise for their work
opts.why: Public praise helps, and it is unaimed. Sponsorship puts a specific name in front of a specific decision.

deeper.title: Sponsorship with a light touch
deeper.body: Giving advocacy has its own craft: vouch for the work, not the whole person. 'I have seen their process mapping and it was excellent' is spendable and survives a miss; 'they are amazing' is a blank check. Match the size of your claim to what you have actually seen, name the evidence, and let the decision-maker do the rest. Small accurate claims, repeated over time, build more careers than one grand endorsement.
steps: Pick one colleague, role only, and write the one-sentence vouch: the specific work you saw and what it tells a decision-maker.
Identify the next room or thread where that sentence would count, and decide now that you will say it there.

opts: Sponsors are always more senior than mentors
Mentoring is formal, sponsorship is informal
A sponsor spends their credibility on you where you are absent
recap.why: Mentoring is advice given to you. Sponsorship costs the sponsor something: their name staked on your work in rooms you never see.

recap.q: What makes someone able to sponsor you safely?
opts: Having seen your finished work up close
recap.why: Sponsors stake reputation on evidence. Show one finished piece of work and how you did it; that is what a sponsor can repeat in a room.

recap.q: You want to give advocacy this month. What is the move?
opts: Post public praise for their work
Say their name, with evidence, where a decision is being made
recap.why: The name plus the work you have seen, in front of someone who decides. Every staff member has rooms where that sentence is theirs to say.

recapMsgs.high: You know the currency. Now spend a little of it on someone.
recapMsgs.mid: Nearly there. Look again at the ask you built, then make your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: Spend a little credibility this week.
capstone.lead: Pick one advocacy move: an ask for yourself or a give for a colleague. Roles only, never names; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: Who is this about? The role, and the work you have seen or want seen.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. research coordinator; ran the event nobody else could have

practices.name: The showing
practices.move: Walk someone senior through one finished piece of your work and how you did it, so backing you gets easy.

practices.name: The direct ask
practices.move: Name the room: ask someone who has seen your work to put your name forward when a specific chance opens.

practices.name: The give
practices.move: Say a colleague's name, with the work you have seen, in the next room where a decision needs one.

whens.out: The move happens this week, done by Friday.
The move happens the next time the right room or conversation opens, and you walk in ready.
The move happens within two weeks, with the date written down today.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did it cost, and what came back?

closing.headline: Advice is free. Back somebody.
closing.lead: You can tell the currencies apart now, and your ask has a room attached. That closes the Retain, Grow, Move week; the advocacy question travels home with you.

facilitator.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; no management experience assumed. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; this session closes the February Retain, Grow, Move week.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the advocacy move on your card happen? What did it cost, and what came back? Whose name do you say in rooms they are not in?' Count of completed advocacy moves is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: Advice versus advocacy
s1.purpose: Install the distinction: mentoring is advice given to you, sponsorship is credibility spent on you.
s1.say: Think about the best career help you ever got. For most of us it was advice: a mentor, a coach, someone generous with guidance. Advice matters, and careers rarely move on advice alone. They move when somebody says your name in a room you are not in and stakes a little of their own reputation on it. That second thing has a name, sponsorship, and the economist Sylvia Ann Hewlett has studied it for over a decade. Her distinction is the one we use all session: a mentor gives you advice; a sponsor spends credibility on you. People who cannot tell the two apart keep asking for advice when what they need is backing.
facilitate: Run Advice or advocacy? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round two, pause on the cost: what does the director risk that the helpful analyst does not?
Run the breakout: was your last real career help advice or advocacy?

ask.q: Why do the kind words in round three feel so much like sponsorship?
expect: They sound like a prediction about your future
ask.respond: Right, and nothing traveled. The test is always the same: did the words reach someone with a decision to make, and did they cost the speaker anything?

s1.debrief: Advice is words to you; advocacy is risk taken for you somewhere you are not. Hewlett's research says careers rarely move on the first alone.
s1.watchFor: People concluding mentors are worthless. Keep both currencies valuable: advice builds the work, advocacy moves it.
s1.transition: So how do you get sponsored? You earn it, then you ask. That is next.
s1.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the ask question.

s2.title: Earning and asking
s2.purpose: Give everyone a concrete path to sponsorship: visible finished work plus a specific, bounded ask.
s2.say: Sponsorship sounds like something that happens to lucky people. It is closer to a transaction with two halves. A sponsor spends reputation, so they need evidence: work they have seen up close. And sponsors are busy, so they need the ask said out loud, with a room attached. Show the work, name the room. People who do both get backed at rates that look like luck from the outside.
facilitate: Run Build the ask; two minutes for both choices, then run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: evidence a sponsor can repeat, an ask with a room attached.

ask.q: What makes the direct ask feel so hard?
expect: It feels like begging for favors
ask.respond: Reframe it: a specific, bounded ask is easy to grant and easy to decline, which makes it respectful in both directions. The vague hope is the real imposition.

s2.debrief: Sponsorable means seen: one finished piece of work, walked through. Asked means named: this room, this chance, my name.
s2.watchFor: People whose ask is really a promotion request. Keep the ask pointed at a specific room or chance, never a title.
s2.transition: You know how to receive it. The last section flips it: you have credibility to spend too.
s2.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

s3.title: Giving it away
s3.purpose: Land the advocacy question and get every person to name, role only, who they advocate for.
s3.say: Here is the part that makes advocacy an everyone skill and never a perk of rank. You sit in rooms other people are absent from every week. When someone asks who could take this on, you have a name you could say and evidence you could attach. Most of us hold that credibility and spend none of it. So the question this section leaves you with is simple: whose name do you say in rooms they are not in?
facilitate: Read the concept card aloud; let the advocacy question sit for a beat.
Show the In the room card, then open the discussion prompt: whose name do you say, roles only? An honest nobody counts; take two or three voices.
Run the breakout: who have you spoken up for lately, roles only; an honest nobody counts.

ask.q: Who advocated for you at some point, and did you know it at the time?
expect: Most found out later or never
A few can name the exact moment
Some are realizing it right now, on the call
ask.respond: That delay is the signature of real sponsorship: it happens where you are not. Someone on this call is that unseen person for a colleague. Be them on purpose.

s3.debrief: Advocacy at any level: a name, the work you have seen, a room where it counts. If your answer to the question is nobody, pick someone this week.
s3.watchFor: Names slipping out in the breakout. Warmly enforce roles only; even praise stays roles-never-names on a group call.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then your advocacy card.
s3.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for advocacy question answers in chat, roles only.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One move: the showing, the ask, or the give. The role and the work, never a name. Build the card, pick the window, and copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday. Two quiet minutes, then we close.
facilitator.closeSay: That closes the Retain, Grow, Move week: Monday gave managers the bench, Tuesday pointed the Talent Marketplace and the Transfer Portal at your own next move, and today gave everyone the human engine under both, advocacy. Make your move this week. If you want more on what keeps people, the LinkedIn Learning course Retaining Your Best Talent by Roberta Matuson, with its navigator-led stay-interview practice lab, runs all month. Next week Anchor's Edge rolls into March and Coaching as the Core Manager Behavior: a fresh Manager Monday, same rhythm, new theme.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Someone names a real colleague during a breakout or share-out
contingencies.then: Protect them warmly and immediately: 'Hold that. Roles, never names.' Advocacy is practiced in real rooms, never rehearsed with real names on a group call.

contingencies.if: A participant says nobody senior has ever seen their work
contingencies.then: Point at the showing move: seen is arranged, never waited for. One finished piece of work, one walk-through, and the evidence problem is solved in thirty minutes.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't asking someone to sponsor me just asking for favoritism?
toughQuestions.a: Favoritism is backing without evidence. Sponsorship is backing built on work the sponsor has actually seen, which is why the showing comes before the ask. You are asking someone to repeat what they know firsthand, and that is how good staffing decisions get made.

toughQuestions.q: I am early in my career. Do I have any credibility to spend on someone else?
toughQuestions.a: You have rooms: team meetings, chats, peers asking who could help. Peer advocacy is real advocacy; a name plus evidence carries weight at every level, and giving it is how you learn to earn it.

toughQuestions.q: What if I sponsor someone and their work disappoints?
toughQuestions.a: That risk is exactly what makes sponsorship valuable, so manage it like a sponsor does: back work you have genuinely seen, be specific about what you are vouching for, and treat one miss as information rather than a reason to stop spending.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Thursday, 45 minutes on advocacy. Come with one piece of your work you are proud of, and one colleague whose work you rate highly. You will never be asked to name them. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the advocacy move happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the move on your card happen? 2) What did it cost, and what came back? 3) Whose name do you say in rooms they are not in?
